source.title: Learning Towards Emergence: Paving the Way to Induce Emergence by Inhibiting Monosemantic Neurons on Pre-trained Models
source.authors: Jia-Chuan Wang; Shimin Di; Tianhao Tang; Hao-Yang Li; Charles Wang Wai Ng; Xiao-Fang Zhou; Lei Chen

page_placements.theme: Neuron importance, monosemanticity and splitting change with language-model scale

record.file_problem: None; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures feature-conditioned neuron statistics and a false-killing proxy in Pythia language models, using MS, sparse probing and labeled feature datasets rather than the original studies’ methods.
record.gate_note: The main findings relevant to the claim are the scale and layer trends in MS and FKR, and the reported dependence on feature datasets. Benchmark accuracy and timing results concern the proposed training method, not whether neurons have unrelated meanings, so they are not recorded as rows. Values shown only in figures are recorded as figure only.
record.test_reason: Section 3 and Appendix B.2 measure feature-conditioned neuron statistics in pre-trained Pythia models from 70M to 6.9B. The measures are MS, K-S statistics and the False Killing Rate (FKR) on labelled feature datasets, and they bear on layer variation (V2) and measurement dependence (V7). The paper's main aim is the L2E training method. Its benchmark results are method performance and are correctly left out.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that MS is a valid monosemanticity measure and that larger models and middle layers are more polysemantic. They caution that results depend heavily on feature-dataset quality. Their main claim is that L2E, which inhibits monosemantic neurons during pretraining, modestly improves benchmark accuracy on Pythia 70M–2.8B.
record.recipe_differences: Uses MS, sparse probing, K-S statistics and FKR on labeled feature datasets, rather than the original sources’ neuron visualizations or SoLU analyses.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature dataset changes the FKR and reliability of the monosemanticity analysis; FKR also varies with model scale and layer. Sparse-probing results on Code Language are reported as anomalous for Pythia 70M.

fits_no_version.finding: K-S statistics, mean top-feature MS across layers (Figs 5, 9), the top-2% MS threshold of baseline Pythia (Fig 12) and FKR all indicate monosemanticity decreasing as Pythia scale grows from 70M to 6.9B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neuron polysemanticity in language models increases with model scale.

record.problems: The authors report dependence on feature-dataset quality, including weak or anomalous probing results on Code Language and poorer discrimination on Data Subset. Most plotted measurements are not numerically tabulated. Main training experiments cover Pythia models only up to 2.8B and 10% of the original training steps; the authors describe the evidence as preliminary.
record.rows_left_out: Benchmark accuracy, timing, inhibition-rate performance comparisons, and ablations of the proposed L2E training method were omitted because they report method performance rather than directly measuring the claim’s neuron-semantic behavior. Other figure-only MS plots across layers (Figures 5 and 9) were omitted as overlapping scale/layer analyses already represented by the K-S and FKR rows.

untested.parts: No direct share of MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens. Only proxies, on Pythia only.
No test of superposition or feature-count versus neuron-count.
No test of initialization, regularization or noise without capacity pressure.
No comparison of activation function or architecture. L2E is deliberate inhibition, measured only by its MS threshold and benchmarks.
No examination of whether mixed neurons share one underlying feature.
Activation-range dependence and explanation-scoring methods are not tested. Only feature-dataset choice is varied.

missing.what: Average F1 of the top-10 sparse-probed neurons per dataset and scale; 70M is much lower on Code Language. Of 37 Code neurons with F1>0.9, 21 are Python-related and none HTML/XML.
Baseline Pythia top-2% MS threshold for the middle two layers falls with scale (70M, 410M, 2.8B).

record.verdict_notes: Row ranges are grouped in row_fixes. MS is a squared-deviation-over-variance score, not a direct polysemanticity test, so all V2 evidence is proxy-based. The record's V7 'supports' label on R34–R45 is removed because those rows validate the metric.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not directly estimate the share of MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts; its measures are feature-dataset-dependent proxies. It tests Pythia models and reported layers, not language models generally.
No test of superposition or whether feature capacity exceeds neuron count.
No test of polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization or training noise when capacity is sufficient.
No comparison of activation functions or architectures, nor a test of reducing polysemanticity across those choices. Layer and scale comparisons alone do not test this version.
No investigation of whether apparently mixed neurons share a feature such as pose or related subfeatures.
The study tests sensitivity to feature datasets and probing results, but not different activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods generally.

rows.subject: Pythia 70M
rows.operation_detail: Compared MS-score distributions for the relatively most monosemantic feature and the universal set using a K-S statistic.
rows.baseline: Universal-set MS scores compared with MS scores for the feature with the highest average score
rows.note: The paper reports that K-S statistics decrease as model scale increases, interpreting this as diminished prominence of the monosemantic set.
rows.check: These K-S rows show monosemanticity falling with model scale. No version claims a scale trend, and a K-S distance between the top-feature MS distribution and the universal set cannot give a share of neurons responding to unrelated contexts. Moved to fits_no_version. For 70M on Code Language (R3) the authors call the results abnormal because probing failed (Fig 10).

rows.subject: Pythia 70M
rows.operation_detail: Compared MS for selected monosemantic neurons on corresponding-feature inputs versus other-feature inputs.
rows.measure: MS on corresponding versus other features
rows.baseline: MS on inputs without the corresponding feature
rows.note: The paper describes significantly different MS values for feature-present and feature-absent inputs.
rows.check: These rows validate the study's MS metric against sparse-probing-selected neurons. They do not test whether neurons are polysemantic or whether the verdict depends on measurement. For 70M on Code Language the authors flag an anomaly, with lower MS for probed neurons (Fig 8b).
